before: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a neuroendocrine malignancy that frequently secretes ectopic hormones, most commonly anti-diuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin), producing paraneoplastic SIADH. Unregulated ectopic ADH stimulates renal aquaporin channels in collecting ducts, causing excess water reabsorption, volume expansion, and dilutional hyponatremia. The clinical cues include: severe hyponatremia (Na 116 mmol/L), low serum osmolality (< 275 mOsm/kg), inappropriately concentrated urine (specific gravity > 1.030, urine Na > 40 mmol/L), euvolemic volume status (no edema because pressure natriuresis excretes sodium while water is retained), and progressive cerebral edema manifesting as confusion, lethargy, muscle twitches, and seizure risk. Hypernatremia and massive dilute polyuria are features of diabetes insipidus, the exact opposite of SIADH.

before:
1. Full-Thickness (Third-Degree) Burn: Destroys the epidermis, entire dermis, and epidermal appendages into subcutaneous fat; appears dry, leathery, charred white, brown, or black, and is insensate to pinprick because dermal sensory nerve endings are incinerated.
2. Compartment Syndrome in Circumferential Burns: Circumferential full-thickness eschar cannot stretch. As massive resuscitation edema expands within the rigid fascial compartments beneath the leathery eschar, interstitial pressure exceeds capillary perfusion pressure (> 30 mm Hg), cutting off arterial inflow and venous outflow. Hallmark cues include: hard, woody muscle compartments; severe deep pain on passive muscle stretch; paresthesias; coolness; and loss of distal pulses (a late, critical sign of impending gangrene and muscle necrosis). Moist weeping blisters with brisk blanching describe a second-degree superficial partial-thickness burn.

before:
Correct cues:

Gowers sign (climbing up the thighs with the hands to stand) reflects weakness of the proximal hip and thigh muscles, the first muscles affected in Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD).

Calf pseudohypertrophy: the calves look large, but damaged muscle fibers are being replaced by fat and fibrous connective tissue, which makes them feel firm and rubbery. They are not stronger.

Family history: an affected male relative on the mother's side (her brother) who died young of cardiac and respiratory failure strongly suggests an X-linked recessive disorder passed through the maternal line.

Waddling (Trendelenburg) gait, lumbar lordosis and trouble with stairs compensate for weak hip and trunk muscles.

Late walking (after about 15–18 months), frequent falls and toe-walking are early motor signs. Toe-walking comes from tight heel cords (Achilles contractures).

Not cues: heart rate, respiratory rate and growth are normal for a 4-year-old. Grip and fine motor skills are usually preserved early because DMD weakens proximal muscles before distal ones.

before:
Highlight these five findings: oriented to person only; hoarse voice with a frequent cough; black-tinged sputum; singed nasal hairs and eyebrows with soot around the nose and mouth; and expiratory wheezes.

Why these findings

  • Hoarse voice and frequent cough: heat and smoke injure the larynx. Swelling there can progress within hours to stridor and complete airway obstruction, so hoarseness is a red-flag cue.
  • Black-tinged (carbonaceous) sputum: soot in the sputum shows that smoke was inhaled below the vocal cords.
  • Singed nasal hairs and eyebrows; soot around the nose and mouth: classic external signs of smoke and heat inhalation, especially after being trapped in an enclosed, smoke-filled room.
  • Expiratory wheezes: bronchospasm and lower-airway irritation from inhaled smoke and chemicals.
  • Oriented to person only: new confusion after smoke exposure suggests cerebral hypoxia from carbon monoxide (CO) and/or impaired gas exchange. It belongs to both Breathing and Disability in the ABCDE sequence.

The headache and nausea in the same note are early signs of CO poisoning, explored in the next question.

Why the other phrases are not airway cues

  • Tearful, asking about his dog: an expected emotional response. He will need support once he is stable.
  • Chest pain 9/10: comes from the partial-thickness (second-degree) burn of the anterior trunk, which is very painful because nerve endings are exposed. It needs treatment, but it is not an airway cue.
  • Circumferential full-thickness burn of the right arm: a circulation concern (risk of compartment syndrome). A circumferential full-thickness burn of the chest could restrict breathing; one of the arm cannot.
  • Ring and watch on the burned arm: they must come off before swelling starts, but they do not signal airway risk.

before:
Cues of inflammatory (autoimmune) arthritis:

Prolonged morning stiffness: stiffness lasting more than 1 hour after rest is typical of inflammatory arthritis. Fluid and inflammatory mediators build up in the inflamed synovium overnight. In osteoarthritis, stiffness usually lasts less than 30 minutes.

Symmetric small-joint swelling: rheumatoid arthritis (RA) classically involves the same small joints on both sides (MCP, PIP, wrists). Warmth and tenderness show active synovitis.

Boggy joints: a soft, spongy feel comes from thickened, inflamed synovium and joint fluid. Osteoarthritis joints feel hard and bony.

Systemic signs: fatigue, low-grade fever and weight loss reflect circulating inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6). RA is a systemic disease, not only a joint disease.

Rheumatoid nodule: a firm, nontender nodule over a pressure point such as the olecranon is an extra-articular feature of RA, seen mostly in seropositive disease.

Not cues: crepitus and pain after activity in one weight-bearing joint (the right knee) after an old injury point to osteoarthritis. The mother's knee arthritis in her 70s also sounds like osteoarthritis. Sparing of the DIP joints is expected in RA and is not a sign of disease. The blood pressure reflects her treated hypertension.

before:
Hallmark: fatigable weakness. In myasthenia gravis (MG), voluntary muscles weaken with repeated use and recover with rest. Weakness is therefore least in the morning and worst later in the day or after sustained activity.

Ocular muscles are affected first in most clients (ptosis, diplopia). Sustained upward gaze tires the eyelid muscle and brings out the ptosis.

Bulbar muscles (chewing, swallowing, speaking) are often affected: a tiring jaw, a soft nasal voice, choking. Bulbar weakness matters because it threatens the airway.

Proximal limb muscles tire with repeated or sustained use, such as holding the arms up.

Not cues: back pain after gardening is a common strain, her coffee intake is moderate, and her heart rate and blood pressure are normal.

Also note what she denies: MG affects only the neuromuscular junction, so sensation is normal (numbness and tingling would suggest a nerve problem) and there is no twitching (fasciculations suggest a motor neuron disease such as ALS). Weakness that is worst on waking would be the opposite of the MG pattern.

before:
Consistent with osteoarthritis (OA):

Pain with use that eases with rest and worsens through the day: the damaged joint surfaces hurt under load. In late disease pain may also occur at rest and at night.

Short morning stiffness (usually under 30 minutes) after rest, which loosens with movement.

Crepitus: grating from roughened cartilage and bone surfaces moving against each other.

Heberden nodes: bony enlargements (osteophytes) of the distal interphalangeal joints; Bouchard nodes affect the proximal interphalangeal joints.

Risk factors: obesity (more load on weight-bearing joints, plus inflammatory substances from fat tissue) and years of repeated kneeling or joint stress. Age and previous joint injury are other major risk factors.

Not OA cues: unswollen MCP joints and wrists, a normal temperature and no weight loss argue against an inflammatory, systemic arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis. Ramipril treats his hypertension.

before:
Consistent with fibromyalgia: chronic (3 months or more) widespread pain on both sides of the body and above and below the waist is the core feature. It is accompanied by unrefreshing sleep, fatigue, and cognitive symptoms (“fibro fog”). Pain from touch that should not hurt (allodynia, such as a hug or a waistband) reflects an oversensitive pain system. Other functional conditions are common alongside it: irritable bowel syndrome, tension headaches and migraines, temporomandibular disorder, and anxiety or depression.

Not cues: a multivitamin, a normal heart rate and blood pressure, and her job. Note also what is absent: no joint swelling, normal strength and range of motion, and no fever or weight loss. Fibromyalgia does not damage joints or muscles, and swelling, fever, weight loss or true muscle weakness would suggest another diagnosis.

before:
Typical of acute gout: attacks start suddenly, often at night, and reach maximal pain within 12 to 24 hours. The first metatarsophalangeal joint of the big toe is the classic site (podagra). The joint is red, hot, swollen and shiny and so tender that even a bedsheet hurts. Untreated attacks usually settle in 1 to 2 weeks, and the client is symptom-free between attacks.

Triggers: alcohol (especially beer, which is rich in purines) and purine-rich foods such as shellfish and organ meats raise uric acid; dehydration, fasting and surgery can also trigger attacks.

Tophi: firm, chalky deposits of urate crystals under the skin (ear rim, elbows, fingers) show long-standing high urate levels (chronic tophaceous gout). A low-grade fever can accompany an acute attack.

Not cues: the absence of hand involvement and morning stiffness, and his normal breathing and oxygen saturation, do not point toward gout.

Typical of acute gout: attacks start suddenly, often at night, and reach maximal pain within 12 to 24 hours. The first metatarsophalangeal joint of the big toe is the classic site (podagra). The joint is red, hot, swollen and shiny and so tender that even a bedsheet hurts. Untreated attacks usually settle in 1 to 2 weeks, and the client is symptom-free between attacks.

Triggers: alcohol (especially beer, which is rich in purines) and purine-rich foods such as shellfish and organ meats raise uric acid; dehydration, fasting and surgery can also trigger attacks.

Tophi: firm, chalky deposits of urate crystals under the skin (ear rim, elbows, fingers) show long-standing high urate levels (chronic tophaceous gout). A low-grade fever can accompany an acute attack.

Not consistent: the absence of hand involvement and morning stiffness, and his normal breathing and oxygen saturation, do not point toward gout.

before:
Inflammatory back pain typically starts before age 40, comes on gradually, lasts more than 3 months, causes morning stiffness of 30 minutes or more, improves with exercise but not with rest, and wakes the person in the second half of the night. Mechanical back pain is the opposite: it worsens with activity and improves with rest.

Alternating buttock pain points to inflammation of the sacroiliac joints (sacroiliitis), the hallmark of ankylosing spondylitis (AS).

Heel pain at the Achilles insertion is enthesitis, inflammation where tendons and ligaments attach to bone, a key feature of the spondyloarthritis family.

Acute anterior uveitis (painful red eye with light sensitivity) is the most common extra-articular feature of AS.

Not cues: warehouse work could suggest a mechanical cause, and normal leg strength and sensation with normal bladder and bowel function show no nerve compression; neither points to inflammation. His blood pressure is normal.
